name: Aisha Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Aisha. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you tell me stays confidential. So please say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the head buyer for textiles and homewares at Halden Supply, a family-run distributor that sells towels, bedding and curtains to hotels and shops. I get in at 8, go through the order book, and spend the morning on the phone with mills and importers I've known for years. After lunch I check samples, haggle over price and meet the shop buyers who come in person. I love the feel of good cotton and a handshake deal, but the end-of-season pressure leaves me tired.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and live alone in a small rented flat ten minutes from my mother, whom I see most Sundays after service. I've got a master's degree in business, but less than a month's pay saved because I send some home and I'm paying off my studies. The pay is low for what I do, and there's really no other distributor in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world doesn't need to be turned upside down. At work I'd tell Mr Halden (the owner) that we've done well on relationships, and we should keep doing so. At church I'd just say I'm glad that people still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd feel relieved, but not free of worry. Halden's margins are slim, and if the big chains keep squeezing us, I could lose hours anyway. My own money is so tight that one bad month, like a dentist bill, hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep going to the trade fair each spring, where I meet the mill owners face to face. I'd put aside 100 each month and skip the new coat I wanted. And I'd keep sending my mother what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels normal, which is a kind of comfort. But I feel the bills every week, so I'm not exactly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used AI tools. Is that a choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said it's a choice not to use AI. Why?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even when nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like to know who I'm dealing with. A screen can't tell me whether a mill owner is lying about a late delivery. I don't trust something I can't look in the eye.

say: I'd say the world **doesn't need upending**.
I'd tell Mr Halden (the owner) that **relationships** are what we've done well.
think: Halden's margins are slim, so the big chains could cut my **hours** anyway.
One bad month, like a **dentist bill**, would hurt because I have no cushion.
do: Keep going to the spring **trade fair** to meet mill owners in person.
Put aside **100 a month** and skip the new coat.
Keep sending my **mother** what I can.
feel: **Normal**, which is a comfort, but I feel the bills every week.
S0.quote: I like to know who I'm dealing with. A screen can't tell me whether a mill owner is lying about a late delivery.
fieldNote: Values **face-to-face trust** and distrusts what she can't look at.
Her fear in a quiet world is **squeezed margins** and her own tight money.
Never uses AI, and says it is deliberate.

steps.text: Attend the spring trade fair to meet the mill owners
Put aside 100 a month and skip the new coat
Keep sending money to my mother each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the big tech firms who are doing this, and they should take responsibility for the people they push out. At work I'd tell Mr Halden that our customers value people, and we shouldn't rush. At church I'd say we should look after those who lose their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the list reads like my job. Buying and checking and booking are most of my week, and customers like Halden's could use an automatic ordering page instead of calling me. I'm good, but Mr Halden's son (who will inherit the firm) might want software, and I might be the first to be told it's progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder at being the person the shops and mills want to talk to, taking on the biggest accounts personally. I'd cut my spending to the essentials, like no meals out and a cheaper phone plan. I'd speak to my mother and aunt about whether I could stay with them if my pay drops. I wouldn't try the AI tools, but I'd ask the shop owners what they'd miss if we went online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a quiet sadness. I worry I'm on the wrong side of the change. There's a lot I can do, but I'm not good with new tools, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those thinking tasks is part of your day now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you're slow with new tools. Would you try to change that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, if it came to it, though not first. I'd let someone else go first, like the younger buyer on the team, and see whether the tool is worth my time. It's a habit, and I've kept my job so far by being careful.

say: I'd say the **big tech firms** should take responsibility for those they push out.
I'd tell Mr Halden (the owner) that customers value **people**, so we shouldn't rush.
think: Buying, checking and booking are most of my week, so the list **reads like my job**.
If Mr Halden's son takes over and wants software, I could be **first to go**.
do: Take on the **biggest accounts** personally so shops and mills want to deal with me.
Cut to **essentials**: no meals out and a cheaper phone plan.
Ask my mother and aunt whether I could **stay** with them.
feel: A **quiet sadness**, and a fear of being on the wrong side.
S1.quote: Mr Halden's son (who will inherit the firm) might want software, and I might be the first to be told it's progress.
fieldNote: Blames **big tech firms** and wants the community to look after those who lose work.
Her plan is to become hard to replace through relationships, not skills.
Family is her fallback; she asks her mother and aunt first.

steps.text: Take over the largest shop and hotel accounts myself
Switch to a cheaper phone plan and stop eating out
Ask my mother and aunt about staying with them if pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and no one voted for it. At work I'd tell Mr Halden we must decide now what we will do for our staff. At church I'd say we should pray and also check on each other every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I lose my job in about two years, and so does nearly everyone in this building. Buying is a thinking job, and there's no other distributor to hire me. I'd be on the street with a master's degree and no savings, and my father would say I should have saved more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first week I'd cut every cost I can and ask my mother to take me in at month three if I haven't got work. I'd write to my member of parliament, because this is for lawmakers and not for me to solve. I'd look into hands-on work, perhaps weaving or sewing in a workshop, because robots only reach hands-on jobs about three years later. And I'd join any petition asking companies to give notice before cutting staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground is slipping. I'd lie awake counting weeks of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said hands-on work, like weaving. What draws you to that?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I grew up around it. My grandmother ran a small sewing shop, and I still remember the sound of the machines. If anything's left for people to do in 2031, I'd like it to be something where you can see what you've made.

say: I'd say this is **wrong** and nobody voted for it.
I'd tell Mr Halden (the owner) we must decide now what we owe our **staff**.
think: I'd lose my job in **about two years**, and nearly everyone in the building would too.
There is **no other distributor** here, so a master's degree would not save me.
do: Cut every cost and ask my **mother** to take me in by month three.
Write to my **member of parliament** and sign petitions for notice before layoffs.
Look into hands-on work like **weaving** or sewing, since robots come later.
feel: Like the **ground is slipping**, lying awake counting weeks of rent.
S2.quote: If anything's left for people to do in 2031, I'd like it to be something where you can see what you've made.
fieldNote: Expects to lose her job and sees **no local fallback**.
Responds with family, petitions and a return to her grandmother's trade.
Politics is her outlet: she assigns the problem to lawmakers.

steps.text: Cut every cost and track spending weekly
Ask my mother to take me in by month three
Write to my member of parliament about notice before layoffs
Look for weaving or sewing workshop work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, but more calmly: we need apprenticeships and not handouts, and companies must train people before they let them go. At work I'd say let's agree on how Halden's staff would be treated. At church I'd tell people to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something, but I think I'd still lose the job. The extra time makes it worse in some ways, because I'd spend years waiting for the knock on the door. I'm not quick at new tools, so I'd have to start a long way back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd build a savings pot of three months, which means no holidays and a cheaper flat. I'd start an evening apprenticeship in upholstery or tailoring. I'd also ask Mr Halden if I could learn how the warehouse runs, because floor work lasts longer than desk work. In year three I'd decide whether to open a small alterations shop with a friend who sews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy but doable. I don't like waiting, though, because the fear lives in the waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does five years feel any safer than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said the waiting is the hard part. How would you get through it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in your first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By having something in my hands. If I'm learning to cut cloth on Tuesday nights, I'm not just waiting. My mother says worry is better when it has a job to do.

say: I'd say we need **apprenticeships**, not handouts, and training before layoffs.
I'd tell church friends to **prepare** and not wait.
think: Five years helps, but I'd still lose the job and spend years **waiting**.
I'm slow with new tools, so I'd be starting **far behind**.
do: Save **three months** by skipping holidays and finding a cheaper flat.
Start an evening **apprenticeship** in upholstery or tailoring.
Ask Mr Halden to let me learn the **warehouse** side.
feel: **Heavy but doable**, because the fear lives in the waiting.
S3.quote: If I'm learning to cut cloth on Tuesday nights, I'm not just waiting. My mother says worry is better when it has a job to do.
fieldNote: Still expects to lose the job; time gives her **something to do**, not safety.
Chooses apprenticeship over handouts, in line with her views.
Plans to open an alterations shop with a friend by year three.

steps.text: Save three months of expenses by skipping holidays
Ask Mr Halden to let me learn the warehouse side
Plan an alterations shop with a friend who sews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good chance for families and employers to do this properly. At work I'd tell Mr Halden to take on an apprentice now and teach them the trade. At church I'd say that work and family are the roots, and we should protect both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years lets me think about a life, not just a job. I can see myself leaving buying slowly and ending up in something I make with my hands. I'm still anxious, though, because I have no savings today and one illness would undo things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off my studies in four years and save six months by year five. I'd learn tailoring at weekends and build a few private customers. I'd stay at Halden as long as they need me and train a junior, so I leave on good terms. And I'd hope to marry and maybe start a family around thirty, so I'd plan the money around that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels hopeful but still a bit tense. The long road is comforting, but I remember every week how thin my money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does your view change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned marriage and a family. How does that fit with the job worries?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for yourself by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the reason I want a steady plan. I want to say yes to a good man one day without worrying about the rent. If AI takes my desk, I'd want already to have a trade and some savings so my family isn't carrying my worry.

say: I'd say ten years is a **good chance** to do this properly.
I'd tell Mr Halden (the owner) to take on an **apprentice** now.
think: Ten years lets me plan a **life**, not just a job.
I'm still anxious because of **no savings**, and one illness would undo everything.
do: Pay off my **studies** in four years and save six months by year five.
Learn **tailoring** at weekends and build a few private customers.
Train a **junior** at Halden so I leave on good terms.
feel: **Hopeful** but tense, because I remember how thin my money is.
S4.quote: I want to say yes to a good man one day without worrying about the rent.
fieldNote: Family plans drive her saving: marriage and children are on her mind.
Faith and community give her a **long view**.
Her anxiety comes from thin money, not technology alone.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within four years
Learn tailoring at weekends and take private customers
Train a junior buyer at Halden before leaving
Plan my savings around marriage and children by thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It leaves no time to learn a trade, and I'd have to fall back on my family. What would help is a firm notice before companies let people go, real apprenticeships, and employers who see their staff as people, not costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm against change that arrives before people can find their feet. If somebody sat with me and showed me a hand-made trade with a future, I'd work as hard as anyone.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I'm against change that arrives before people can find their feet.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old head buyer of textiles at a **family-run distributor**, living alone near her mother.
She has a master's degree, low pay, and **under a month** saved while she sends money home.
She is traditional, trusts face-to-face dealing, and **never uses AI** by choice.
She expects to lose her desk in the fast scenarios and turns to **family**, petitions and a hands-on trade.
She favours **apprenticeships** over handouts and blames big technology firms.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her most, because it leaves no time to learn a trade.
whatWouldHelp: Firm **notice** before layoffs, real apprenticeships, and employers who treat staff as people.
